rv.q: But the genius of the show’s presentation  derived from a 2007 production by Mr. Armfield with Mr. Rush in Melbourne, Australia  is in its use of rowdy comic grotesquerie to lure us into raw and very real emotional territory.

Geoffrey Rush, making his Broadway debut, manages a mesmerizing high-wire act of balancing outrageous comedy and overwhelming tragedy in a fascinating revival of Eugene Ionesco's absurdist 'Exit the King.'
Geoffrey Rush delivers an astonishing performance as the dying monarch in 'Exit the King.'
Rush is never less than virtuosic without lapsing into showboating.
"And later, when the king realizes, "One can't live badly - it's a contradiction in terms," the play feels not just absurd, but absurdly wise.'

His vivid portrayal of human frailties is simply sensational as he takes us on an insightful journey to his ultimate acceptance of his eminent death.
Regardless, Ionesco's account of a ruler who squanders his time is well worth yours.
He commands the stage from the opening to his final spotlighted death throes, toggling easily between tragedy and comedy, not to mention between high comedy and low.

cn.t: Geoffrey Rush delivers a mesmerizing, towering performance in this acclaimed revival of Ionesco's absurdist masterpiece, balancing outrageous comedy and overwhelming tragedy with pure genius in a rarely seen but essential theatrical experience.

vs.sum: The Ethel Barrymore Theatre offers good sightlines with a well-raked mezzanine and minimal obstructions, though some box seats have limited views. Sound quality is average, with some reports of less than ideal acoustics. Comfort is typical for a Broadway theater, with decent legroom in some areas. However, facilities are lacking, with only one restroom on the lower level leading to potential congestion.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.
